data.stimulus:
Arrays (4%)

Let \(A[0:4] = \langle 8, 2, 9, 5, 4 \rangle\) and \(B[1:5] = \langle 5, 4, 1, 2, 3 \rangle\). What is \(A[3 \cdot B[4]-3]\)?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Arrays (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We first find \(B[4]\), which is \(2\). We then find \(A[3 \cdot B[4] - 3] = A[3]\), which is \(5\).

data.stimulus:
Peaks in an array (4%)

Which indices are peaks in the following array: \(A[0:4] = [2,8,8,9,1]\)? Recall that an index \(i\) is a peak if \(A[i]\) is greater than or equal to all of its neighboring elements (each element has one or two neighbors).

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Peaks in an array (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Here \(A[1]=8\) is greater than \(A[0]=2\) and equal to \(A[2]=8\), and \(A[3]=9\) is greater than \(A[2]=8\) and \(A[4]=1\). Hence \(1\) and \(3\) are peaks.

data.stimulus:
Combinatorics (4%)

In how many different ways can we choose \(k\) elements from a set with \(n\) elements, when the order does not matter and we may not choose the same element more than once?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Combinatorics (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The correct answer is the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!k!}\), which is exactly the number of subsets of size \(k\) of a set of size \(n\).

options.label: Every key is equally likely to be mapped to each entry of the hash table, independently of where the other keys are mapped.
If you compute the hash value of the same key several times, you almost always get different results.
The hash function is fast to compute.

data.stimulus:
Hashing (4%)

Which of the following properties are desirable for a hash function?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Hashing (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
1. We want the keys to be spread evenly over the hash table, and the positions of the keys should not depend on each other, so we want property (1).
  2. We gain nothing from continuity of a hash function, so (2) is irrelevant.
  3. A hash function must always give the same result for the same key, so (3) is wrong.
  4. Finally, we want the hash function to be fast to compute, so (4) is correct.

data.stimulus:
Properties of binary search trees (4%)

Which of the following statements describe properties of a binary search tree?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Properties of binary search trees (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: A binary search tree has at most two children per node, and the key of the left child is less than or equal to the key of the node. The numbers of nodes in the left and right subtrees can vary, so the left subtree does not always have fewer nodes. The height is not always \(O(\log n)\); this only holds for balanced trees. Every node has exactly one parent, except the root, which has none.

data.stimulus:
Symmetric relation (4%)

Let \(X\) be a set and let \(R \subseteq X \times X\) be a relation on \(X\). What is the definition of \(R\) being symmetric?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Symmetric relation (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: A relation \(R\) is symmetric if for all \(a,b \in X\): \((a,b) \in R \implies (b,a) \in R\). The other statements do not describe symmetry.

data.stimulus:
Asymptotic analysis (4%)

Consider the function \[\begin{aligned} f(x) = x^{3}\log x + 7x^{2} + 10x. \end{aligned}\] Which of the following statements about \(f\) are correct?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Asymptotic analysis (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The dominant term of \(f\) is \(x^{3}\log x\), so \(f = O(x^{3}\log x)\) and \(f = O(x^{4})\). Since \(f\) grows faster than \(x^{3}\), we have \(f = \Omega(x^{3})\). Since the dominant term is \(x^{3}\log x\), we have \(f = \Theta(x^{3}\log x)\).

data.stimulus:
RAM model (4%)

Which of the following operations take constant time in the RAM model? Assume that \(a,b\) are integer variables and \(A\) is an array.

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: RAM model (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
• The first operation takes \(O(n)\) time, since both an addition and an array lookup must be performed \(n\) times.
  • A subtraction takes constant time \(O(1)\).
  • A single lookup in \(A\) takes \(O(1)\) time.
  • \(a^{3}\) is a constant number of multiplications, so the lookup \(A[a^3]\) also takes constant time \(O(1)\).
  • \(b^{a}\) may take \(\log a\) multiplications in the worst case.

data.stimulus:
Sets and integers (4%)

Let \(A = \{5, 10, 2026\}\) and \(B = \{5k \mid k \in \{1,\dots,500\}\}\). Which of the following statements are true?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Sets and integers (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: \(\sum_{a \in A} a=5+10+2026=2041\). \(\text{GCD}(B)=5\). \(\sum_{b \in B-A} b=\sum_{b \in B} b-5-10\); we should not subtract 2026 as is done in the expression \(\sum_{b \in B} b-\sum_{a \in A} a\). Since \(2026\notin B\), it is not the case that \(A \subseteq B\). We have \(\sum_{b \in B} b=\sum_{k=1}^{500} 5k=5\sum_{k=1}^{500} k=5\cdot 250\cdot 501\).

data.stimulus:
Modular arithmetic (4%)

Recall that for integers \(a\) and \(n\) we use the notation \(a\text{ mod }n\) to denote the remainder of \(a\) modulo \(n\). What is the value of the following expression? \[\begin{aligned} (58\text{ mod }8) \cdot \left((5214\text{ mod }4)+ (8627\text{ mod }5)\right) \end{aligned}\]

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Modular arithmetic (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We have \(58\text{ mod }8 = 2\), \(5214\text{ mod }4 = 2\) and \(8627\text{ mod }5 = 2\). So the expression evaluates to \(2 \cdot (2 + 2) = 8\).

Max-Heap (4%)

You run BUILD-MAX-HEAP on the array \(A = \langle 3, 1, 6, 5, 2, 4 \rangle\). Which heap do you get as the result?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Max-Heap (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: When BUILD-MAX-HEAP is run bottom-up on the array, the largest value is moved to the root, and the heap property is restored recursively for all subtrees. The final array is \(\langle 6, 5, 4, 1, 2, 3 \rangle\), where no node has a child with a larger value than itself.

data.stimulus:
Array representation of a linked list (4%)

Which singly linked list \(L\) is represented by this array \(A\)? The pointer \(L.\text{head}\) (i.e., the index of the first list element) is stored in \(A[0]\). Each list element is stored in two adjacent fields \(A[i]\) and \(A[i+1]\), where \(A[i]\) contains the key and \(A[i+1]\) contains a pointer (index) to the next list element.

\[\begin{aligned} A[0:10] = \langle 4, 0, 3, 7, 10, 2, 0, 8, 9, 5, \text{NIL} \rangle \end{aligned}\]

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Array representation of a linked list (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
The pointer \(L.\text{head}\) is stored in \(A[0]\), so we start at index \(4\).

  • At index \(4\) we find the key \(A[4] = 10\) and the pointer \(A[5] = 2\).
  • At index \(2\) we find the key \(A[2] = 3\) and the pointer \(A[3] = 7\).
  • At index \(7\) we find the key \(A[7] = 8\) and the pointer \(A[8] = 9\).
  • At index \(9\) we find the key \(A[9] = 5\) and the pointer \(A[10] = \text{NIL}\), so the list ends here.

Hence the array represents the list \[\begin{aligned} 10 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 5. \end{aligned}\]

An infinite loop occurs during the insertion, so a rehash will take place.

data.stimulus:
Cuckoo hashing (4%)

In the hash table below, 5 keys have been inserted using cuckoo hashing. Each key has two possible positions; the arrows show the alternative position of each key, so, e.g., \(A\) can be moved between positions \(0\) and \(1\), \(B\) between \(1\) and \(2\), etc.

We now want to insert a new key \(K\) with possible positions \[\begin{aligned} h_{1}(K) = 5, \qquad h_{2}(K) = 4. \end{aligned}\]

What is the final state of the hash table after inserting \(K\)?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Cuckoo hashing (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
The insertion proceeds as follows:

  • \(K\) is inserted at position \(5\), so \(E\) is evicted to its alternative position \(3\).
  • \(E\) is inserted at position \(3\), so \(D\) is evicted to its alternative position \(0\).
  • \(D\) is inserted at position \(0\), so \(A\) is evicted to its alternative position \(1\).
  • \(A\) is inserted at position \(1\), so \(B\) is evicted to its alternative position \(2\).
  • \(B\) is inserted at position \(2\), so \(C\) is evicted to its alternative position \(3\).
  • \(C\) is inserted at position \(3\), so \(E\) is evicted to its alternative position \(5\)
  • \(E\) is inserted at position \(5\), so \(K\) is evicted to its alternative position \(4\), which is empty. Since \(K\) is placed in an empty slot, the insertion stops here.

The final table is therefore \[\begin{aligned} \langle D, A, B, C, K, E \rangle. \end{aligned}\]

data.stimulus:
Functions (4%)

Which of the following functions \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) are bijections?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Functions (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: \(x^{2}\) is not injective, since \((-1)^2 = 1^2 = 1\). \(|x|\) is not injective, since \(|-1|=|1|=1\). \(x^{3}\) is both injective and surjective, and hence bijective. \(e^{x}\) is not surjective, since there is no \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(e^{x} < 0\). \(2x + \sin(x)\) is both injective (since its derivative is \(2 + \cos(x)\geq 1> 0\)) and surjective, and hence bijective.

data.stimulus:
Matrix computation (4%)

Let \[\begin{aligned} A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix},\quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix},\quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2\\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}\] Compute the expression \(A B + A C\).

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Matrix computation (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
We can use distributivity:

\[\begin{aligned} A B + A C = A(B + C). \end{aligned}\]

Since \(B + C = I_2\), we get \[\begin{aligned} A(B + C) = A \cdot I_2 = A. \end{aligned}\] Thus

\[\begin{aligned} A B + A C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}\]

If we instead compute directly: \[\begin{aligned} AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad AC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2\\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2\\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \end{aligned}\]

and hence

\[\begin{aligned} AB + AC = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2\\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \end{aligned}\]

data.stimulus:
Poker hands (4%)

We play with a standard deck of 52 playing cards (4 suits and 13 ranks). A hand consists of 5 cards drawn at random without replacement. How many hands are there of the following type:

  • Three of the cards have the same rank.
  • The remaining two cards have other ranks, but the same suit as each other.

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Poker hands (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The three cards of the same rank can be chosen in \(13\cdot \binom{4}{3}\) ways. The suit of the remaining cards can be chosen in 4 ways, and then we must choose 2 of the 12 remaining ranks. This gives \(13\cdot \binom{4}{3}\cdot 4\cdot \binom{12}{2}\).

data.stimulus:
Expected Value (4%)

Let \(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, X_{4}\) be the outcomes of four independent rolls of a standard six-sided die. What is the expected value of \((X_{1} + X_{2})\cdot (X_{3}+X_{4})\)?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Expected Value (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Since \(X_{1} + X_{2}\) and \(X_{3} + X_{4}\) depend on different die rolls, they are independent, so the expected value is the product of their expected values: \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[(X_{1} + X_{2}) \cdot ( X_{3} + X_{4})] = \mathbb{E}[X_{1} + X_{2}] \cdot \mathbb{E}[ X_{3} + X_{4}] = (\mathbb{E}[X_{1}] + \mathbb{E}[X_{2}]) \cdot (\mathbb{E}[ X_{3}] + \mathbb{E}[X_{4}]) \end{aligned}\] Since the expected value of a single roll of a six-sided die is \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] &= \frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6} = 3.5 \end{aligned}\] we get the result \[\begin{aligned} \left( 3.5 + 3.5\right)^{2} = 7^{2} = 49. \end{aligned}\]

data.stimulus:
Dijkstra's algorithm (4%)

Consider the following weighted, directed graph:

Suppose Dijkstra's algorithm is used to find the shortest distances from vertex \(A\) to all vertices in the graph. State the order in which the vertices are extracted from the priority queue in Dijkstra's algorithm.

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Dijkstra's algorithm (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
• Start: \(d(A)=0\), all others \(\infty\).
  • From \(A\): \(d(B)=4\), \(d(C)=1\). The next vertex is \(C\) (smallest distance).
  • From \(C\): \(d(B)\) is improved to \(1+1=2\), \(d(D)=1+4=5\).
  • The next vertex is \(B\) (distance \(2\)), which gives \(d(E)=1+1+2=4\).
  • The next vertex is \(E\) (distance \(4\)).
  • The last vertex is \(D\) (distance \(5\)).

The order is therefore \(A,C,B,E,D\).

data.stimulus:
Recurrence (4%)

Consider the following recurrence: \[\begin{aligned} T(0) & = 1 \\ T(n) & = 2T(n-1) + 1 \quad \text{for } n \geq 1. \end{aligned}\] Which of the following functions solves the recurrence?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Recurrence (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We have \(2^{0+1}-1 = 1\), so \(2^{n+1}-1\) satisfies the initial condition. Furthermore, we see that \[\begin{aligned} 2^{n+1}-1 = 2 \cdot 2^{n} - 1 = 2 \cdot \left( 2^{n} - 1\right) + 1, \end{aligned}\] which shows that the function satisfies the recurrence.
